steps: Identify the shape (or split a compound shape)
Substitute the values (check you're using the perpendicular height)
Calculate and include units (cm², m², etc.)
method_card.title: How to Find Area & Perimeter
method_card.content:
Key area formulas:

$$\text{Rectangle} = l \times w \qquad \text{Triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times b \times h \qquad \text{Parallelogram} = b \times h$$

$$\text{Trapezium} = \frac{1}{2}(a + b) \times h \qquad \text{Circle} = \pi r^2 \qquad \text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = \pi d$$

For compound shapes, split into simpler shapes and add (or subtract) their areas. Always use the perpendicular height, not the slant height.
method_card.example:
Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm.

\(A = \frac{1}{2}(6 + 10) \times 4 = \frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 4 = 32\) cm²

gold.display: A running track is two straight sides of 100 m and two semicircular ends of diameter 60 m. Find the total perimeter to the nearest metre.

misconceptions.note: Student uses radius (30) instead of diameter (60) for the circular perimeter: π × 30 ≈ 94.2 m. Total = 200 + 94 = 294 m. Note: the stored solution message itself uses an incorrect rounded value (≈ 389 rather than 388); see dispute.
misconceptions.message: Two straights = 200 m. Two semicircles = one full circle = π × 60 ≈ 188.5. Total ≈ 389 m.

gold.display: A sector has radius 8 cm and angle \(135°\). Find the area to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student uses 135/180 (half-turn) instead of 135/360 (full turn): (135/180) × π × 64 = 0.75 × 64π ≈ 150.8 cm².

gold.display: A circle has area \(200\) cm². Find the circumference to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student skips the square root step: treats r = 200/π ≈ 63.66, then C = 2π × 63.66 ≈ 400.0 cm.

gold.display: A sector has arc length 12 cm and radius 9 cm. Find the sector angle to the nearest degree.

misconceptions.note: Student omits the factor of 2 in arc length formula, using arc = (θ/360) × πr instead of 2πr: θ = 12 × 360 / (9π) ≈ 152.8° ≈ 153°.

gold.display: An annulus (ring) has outer radius 10 cm and inner radius 6 cm. Find the area to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student subtracts radii before squaring: π(10−6)² = π × 16 ≈ 50.3 cm².

bronze.display: Find the area of a rectangle with length 9 cm and width 5 cm.

misconceptions.note: Student uses perimeter formula instead of area: 2(9+5) = 28. Alternatively expect=14 if they just add two sides (9+5). Most common substitution error: perimeter 2(l+w)=28.

bronze.display: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 12 cm and width 7 cm.

misconceptions.note: Student adds only two sides (one length + one width) without doubling: 12+7 = 19.

bronze.display: Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm.

misconceptions.note: Student omits the ½: 10 × 6 = 60.
misconceptions.message: Don't forget to halve! A = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².

bronze.display: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and height 5 cm.

misconceptions.note: Student applies triangle formula to parallelogram: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20.

bronze.display: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 14 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student uses radius instead of diameter (halves the diameter): C = π × 7 ≈ 22.0 cm.

bronze.display: Find the area of a circle with radius 5 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student forgets to square the radius: A = π × 5 ≈ 15.7 cm².

bronze.display: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and height 6 cm.

misconceptions.note: Student omits the ½ in the trapezium formula: (5+9) × 6 = 84.

bronze.display: A square has perimeter 48 cm. Find its area.

misconceptions.note: Student confuses area with perimeter: outputs 48 (the perimeter) as the area, failing to find the side length and square it.

silver.display: Find the area of a circle with diameter 18 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student uses diameter as radius: A = π × 18² = π × 324 ≈ 1017.9 cm².
misconceptions.message: r = 9. A = π × 81 ≈ 254.5 cm². Remember to halve the diameter for the radius.

silver.display: A circle has circumference 31.4 cm. Find the radius to 1 d.p. (Use \(\pi = 3.14\))

misconceptions.note: Student divides by π only instead of 2π, finding diameter: 31.4 ÷ 3.14 = 10.0 (reports diameter as radius).

silver.display: An L-shaped room is made of two rectangles: 8 m × 4 m and 3 m × 5 m. Find the total area.

misconceptions.note: Pattern 'wrong_formula' for a compound-area addition is non-specific. Common errors: multiplying instead of adding (32 × 15 = 480), or using wrong rectangle dimensions (e.g. 8×5 + 3×4 = 52). No single determinate wrong answer; expect = null.

silver.display: Find the area of a quarter circle with radius 10 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student forgets to take a quarter and uses full circle area: π × 100 ≈ 314.2 cm².

silver.display: A trapezium has area 60 cm², parallel sides 8 cm and 12 cm. Find the height.

misconceptions.note: Student omits the ½ when rearranging: h = 60 ÷ (8+12) = 60 ÷ 20 = 3.

silver.display: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with radius 7 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student calculates only the curved arc and forgets to add the diameter (straight edge): πr ≈ 22.0 cm.
misconceptions.message: Curved part = πr = 7π ≈ 22.0 cm. Add diameter = 14. Total ≈ 36.0 cm.

silver.display: The area of a circle is 50.3 cm². Find the radius to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.note: Student stops at r² and does not take the square root: reports 16.0 (or 16.01) as the radius.

worked_examples.question: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 8 cm.
Find the area of a circle with radius 7 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
A semicircle has diameter 10 cm. Find its perimeter to 1 d.p.
